sections.title: Mental model — XOR is a cancel-machine

blocks.md: **XOR laws: a^a=0 · a^0=a · commutative+associative. Pairs annihilate in ANY order; loners survive.**

items.title: Single Number I

solutionCode.label: XOR annihilates pairs regardless of order
solutionCode.py:
def single_number(a: list) -> int:
    acc = 0
    for x in a:
        acc ^= x                 # every duplicate cancels itself
    return acc
# WHY ORDER-FREE: XOR is commutative and associative, so the array can be
# reordered arbitrarily. Every pair collapses via x^x == 0, and 0^y == y
# leaves the lone element standing.

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1). Beats the hash-set solution on memory and the sort solution on time.

followups.q: Give the commutativity sentence.
followups.a: "XOR is commutative and associative, so I can mentally reorder the array to group each duplicate pair together; every pair XORs to zero, and zero XOR the survivor is the survivor." That single sentence is the whole proof, and it is what the interviewer is listening for.

followups.q: What breaks if elements appear three times instead of twice?
followups.a: x^x^x is x, not 0, so triples do not cancel. You need bitwise counting mod 3 — accumulate each bit position's count modulo 3 and rebuild the answer, which is LeetCode 137. The XOR trick is specific to pairing.

items.title: Number of 1 Bits — Kernighan edition
items.statement: Loop erases lowest bit per iteration.

solutionCode.label: Kernighan: n & (n-1) erases the lowest set bit
solutionCode.py:
def hamming_weight(n: int) -> int:
    n &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1               # each pass removes exactly one set bit
        count += 1
    return count
# TRACE with n = 12 (1100):
#   n-1 = 1011, n & (n-1) = 1000, count = 1
#   n-1 = 0111, n & (n-1) = 0000, count = 2
# WHY: subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and sets every bit BELOW it
# to 1. The AND keeps only the bits above, so exactly one 1 vanishes.

items.complexity: O(number of SET bits) rather than O(width). For 8 (one set bit) it is one iteration instead of 32.

followups.q: Why does n & (n-1) remove exactly one bit?
followups.a: Write n as (prefix)(1)(zeros). Subtracting 1 borrows through the zeros, giving (prefix)(0)(ones). ANDing the two keeps the untouched prefix and zeros everything from the lowest set bit down — so precisely that one bit is cleared and nothing else changes.

followups.q: When would the naive shift loop still be preferable?
followups.a: When the value is dense — 0xFFFFFFFF costs 32 iterations either way — or when you need to know WHERE the bits are, not just how many. Kernighan tells you the count without revealing positions unless you also track n & -n each round.

items.title: Power of Two — one-liner

solutionCode.label: a power of two has exactly one set bit
solutionCode.py:
def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0
# The n > 0 guard is LOAD-BEARING:
#   n == 0 -> 0 & -1 == 0, so without it zero wrongly passes.
#   n < 0  -> in fixed width, INT_MIN has a single set bit and would pass too.

items.complexity: O(1) — two comparisons and one AND.

followups.q: Why is the guard load-bearing rather than defensive?
followups.a: Zero passes the bit test: 0 & (0-1) is 0 & -1, which is 0. Without n > 0 the function claims 0 is a power of two. In fixed-width C++, INT_MIN (1 followed by 31 zeros) also has exactly one set bit and would pass. Both are wrong answers, not edge-case crashes.

followups.q: How do you extend it to powers of four?
followups.a: A power of four is a power of two whose single bit sits at an EVEN position. Add a mask: n & 0x55555555 must be non-zero, where 0x55555555 has 1s at all even positions. So the test becomes n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) == 0 && (n & 0x55555555) != 0.

items.title: Find the Difference
items.statement: t = shuffled s + extra char; find extra.

solutionCode.label: XOR everything from both strings; only the extra survives

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1). The hash-count solution is O(n) space; sorting is O(n log n).

followups.q: Why does XOR-ing across two different strings work?
followups.a: The accumulator does not care which string a character came from. Since t is a shuffle of s plus one extra, every character except the extra appears an even number of times overall and cancels. It is Single Number with the input split across two containers.

followups.q: Would a sum work instead of XOR?
followups.a: Yes — sum(t) minus sum(s) gives the extra character's code, and it is equally O(n)/O(1). XOR is preferred because it cannot overflow: summing a long string of high-codepoint characters could exceed the type, while XOR stays within the character width by construction.

items.title: Hamming Distance

solutionCode.label: XOR marks the differing positions, then count them
solutionCode.py:
def hamming_distance(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    diff = (x ^ y) & 0xFFFFFFFF   # 1 exactly where the two differ
    count = 0
    while diff:
        diff &= diff - 1          # Kernighan: one iteration per differing bit
        count += 1
    return count
# bin(x ^ y).count("1") is the idiomatic Python one-liner.

items.complexity: O(1) with a hardware popcount, O(number of differing bits) with Kernighan.

followups.q: Why is XOR the right operator for "how many positions differ"?
followups.a: XOR yields 1 exactly when its two inputs disagree and 0 when they agree — it is the bitwise not-equal. So x ^ y is a mask of the differing positions, and Hamming distance is just its population count. That decomposition is why this problem is a two-liner.

followups.q: Where does Hamming distance actually matter?
followups.a: Error-correcting codes size their redundancy by the minimum Hamming distance between valid codewords — distance d detects d-1 errors and corrects floor((d-1)/2). It also underpins locality-sensitive hashing and near-duplicate detection via SimHash.

items.title: Number Complement
items.statement: Flip within USED bit-length only (5→010 flip→101=2).
hints: Build mask of used width: while(m<n) m=(m<<1)|1.

solutionCode.label: build a mask of the USED width, then XOR

items.complexity: O(log n) to build the mask, O(1) for the flip.

followups.q: Why is ~num wrong?
followups.a: The bitwise NOT flips all 32 bits, including the leading zeros that are not part of the number's written form. ~5 becomes -6, not 2. The problem defines the complement only over the bits the value actually occupies, so the mask must be trimmed to that width first.

followups.q: Why does the mask loop use < rather than <=?
followups.a: It must stop as soon as the mask covers num's width. With <=, an exact power-of-two-minus-one input like 7 (111) would grow the mask one bit too far to 1111, flipping 7 into 8 instead of 0. Testing < leaves the mask exactly as wide as num.

items.title: Binary Number with Alternating Bits
hints: n^(n>>1) becomes ALL ones iff alternating.
Then power-of-two check! Two tricks chained.

solutionCode.label: two tricks chained: XOR-shift, then power-of-two-minus-one
solutionCode.py:
def has_alternating_bits(n: int) -> bool:
    # If bits alternate, every adjacent pair differs, so XOR with the shifted
    # value produces a run of ALL ones: 101 ^ 010 == 111.
    x = n ^ (n >> 1)
    # A run of all ones is one less than a power of two, so x & (x+1) == 0.
    return (x & (x + 1)) == 0

followups.q: Walk the two tricks separately.
followups.a: First, n ^ (n >> 1) compares each bit with its neighbour: the result has a 1 wherever adjacent bits differ. Alternating bits means they ALWAYS differ, so the result is a solid run of 1s. Second, a solid run of 1s is 2^k - 1, so adding 1 gives a single set bit and x & (x+1) is 0 — the same identity as X203, shifted by one.

followups.q: Why x & (x+1) rather than the usual x & (x-1)?
followups.a: x & (x-1) == 0 tests for a power of two (one set bit). Here x is a power of two MINUS one (all bits set below some position), so the corresponding identity is x & (x+1) == 0. Reaching for the familiar form is the mistake this problem punishes.

items.title: Two Odd Occurring Numbers
items.statement: Exactly two elements appear odd times; find both.
hints: Split array by any set bit of that mix (lowest).

solutionCode.label: XOR everything, then split the array on a bit where the two differ

items.complexity: Time O(n) in two passes, space O(1). A hash-count solution is O(n) space.

followups.q: Why does splitting on a differing bit work?
followups.a: Every duplicate pair has identical bits, so both copies land in the same bucket and cancel there. p and q differ at the chosen bit, so they land in DIFFERENT buckets. Each bucket therefore reduces to a Single Number problem, and XOR-ing it yields one of the answers.

followups.q: What does mix & (-mix) compute, and why the lowest bit?
followups.a: Two's complement means -mix is ~mix + 1, so ANDing keeps exactly the lowest set bit. Any differing bit would work; the lowest is simply the cheapest to isolate. What matters is that the bit is set in mix, which guarantees p and q are separated.

items.title: XOR of 1..N and Range Queries
items.statement: Implement f(n) four-case; answer q ranges in O(1).

solutionCode.label: XOR of 1..n has a period-4 closed form

items.complexity: O(1) per query after no preprocessing at all — the formula is closed-form.

followups.q: Why does the pattern have period 4?
followups.a: Any four consecutive integers 4k, 4k+1, 4k+2, 4k+3 differ only in their low two bits, which run 00, 01, 10, 11 and XOR to 0, while the identical high bits cancel in pairs. So each aligned block of four contributes nothing, and only the leftover 0 to 3 numbers matter.

followups.q: Why is the range formula a XOR rather than a subtraction?
followups.a: XOR is its own inverse: f(r) already contains f(l-1) as a prefix, and XOR-ing it again cancels it exactly. Prefix sums use subtraction because addition's inverse is subtraction; prefix XORs use XOR because that is what undoes XOR. Same prefix technique, different group operation.

items.title: Counting Bits 0..n (pattern hunt)
hints: Dropping last bit halves the number — reuse its answer.

solutionCode.label: reuse the answer for i >> 1, then add back the dropped bit
solutionCode.py:
def count_bits(n: int) -> list:
    bits = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)   # i>>1 is solved; add back the lost bit
    return bits
# WHY: dropping the last bit of i gives i >> 1, whose popcount is already known
# because i >> 1 < i. The only bit lost is i & 1, so the recurrence is exact and
# each entry costs O(1) -- dynamic programming in one line.

items.complexity: Time O(n) with one array pass. The naive popcount-per-number is O(n log n).

followups.q: Why is bits[i >> 1] guaranteed to be computed already?
followups.a: For i >= 1, i >> 1 is strictly less than i, and the loop fills indices in increasing order. So every value the recurrence reads has already been written. That ordering argument is what makes a bottom-up DP valid, and it is worth stating rather than assuming.

followups.q: What is the alternative recurrence?
followups.a: bits[i] = bits[i & (i-1)] + 1, using Kernighan's identity — the value with its lowest set bit removed, plus one for that bit. Equally O(n) and equally correct. Both work because they reduce i to a strictly smaller already-computed index; which one you pick is taste.
